entries.text: TL;DR: We are enabling the parallel frontend of the Rust compiler on nightly by default, to find remaining issues in preparation for its stabilization. Context The Rust compiler has been using multiple threads to compile code in its "backend" part (using LLVM) for a long time. However, its "frontend" part (which includes type checking and borrow checking) has been executing sequentially, on a single thread, which of course limits the performance of the compiler. If you are interested in a more in-depth explanation of parallelism in the Rust compiler, see this previous post. The compiler frontend actually had support for running in parallel for a long time, but it was not enabled by default due to various issues. Three years ago, we made it possible to opt into the parallel frontend on the nightly channel, with the plan to stabilize it in 2024. Clearly, we did not achieve that goal, but work on the parallel frontend was still slowly progressing in the meantime. Last year, Vadim Petrochenkov, together with several other contributors, started a coordinated effort to finally get the parallel frontend over the finish line. Since then, many long-standing issues were fixed, and its performance was improved. Now we are at a point where we would like to make it widely available. But before that, we want to find out if people encounter issues with it in the wild, which is why we are enabling it by default only on the nightly channel. entries.text: The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.100.0 with: $ rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0. If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across! What's in 1.100.0 stable Never type Allocator API DropGuard API Conjuring zero-sized types Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo min-publish-age Stabilized APIs Never type After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable! This also completes the project goal for this work. The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return, break, and std::process::exit, also have the type !. entries.summary: The Rust Project participated in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for the third time this year. This time we had 13 projects, and our dear contributors have been working very hard on them for several months.
entries.text: The Rust Project participated in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for the third time this year. This time we had 13 projects, and our dear contributors have been working very hard on them for several months. As usual, the projects had various durations, so while some of them have ended in August, the last one has only finished in November, so we have been waiting until we have all the results before publishing this blog post. We are very happy to announce that all 13 projects were successful and passed their final evaluation! We consider it to be a testament to the diligence of our contributors, and the helpfulness of our mentors, that we are able to keep a very high rate[1] of successful GSoC projects several years in a row. At the start of summer, we had a video call with our contributors, so that we could all get to know each other a bit, and learn about their projects. Over the following few months, we continuously communicated with the contributors, provided guidance and answered their questions and reviewed their pull requests. And most importantly, we learned many new things together! It was an overall great experience. We are grateful for all Rust contributions done by our GSoC participants and for the time we spent working together, and we hope that we will continue seeing at least some of them around in the future. entries.text: The rustup team has published a new point release of rustup, 1.29.3. Rustup is the recommended tool to install Rust, a programming language that empowers everyone to build reliable and efficient software. What's new in rustup 1.29.3 This new patch release has fixed some minor regressions over the previous one: Fixed "Illegal instruction" error on certain x86_64 CPUs without SSE4.1. pr#5162 Fixed "lock() not supported" error on Solaris. pr#5167 Further details are available in the changelog! How to update If you have a previous version of rustup installed, getting the new one is as easy as stopping any programs which may be using rustup (e.g. closing your IDE) and running: $ rustup self update Rustup will also automatically update itself at the end of a normal toolchain update: $ rustup update For this particular release, if you have encountered any issues during self-update, you may try to update rustup manually by following the steps below: Download the corresponding rustup-init binary for your platform. Make double sure that no other rustup processes are running. Replace your existing rustup binary with the downloaded rustup-init renamed to rustup. As a reminder, this binary is often located at $HOME/.cargo/bin/rustup, or $CARGO_HOME/bin/rustup if you have overridden the $CARGO_HOME environment variable. entries.text: TLDR: To fund general maintenance, donate to the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund or sponsor the RustNL Maintainers Team To fund specific features and improvements, sponsor fundable Rust Project Goals To fund individual contributors, donate to their GitHub Sponsors accounts There is always so much to do in the Rust Project! New features to implement, bugs to fix, performance optimizations to make, issues to triage… It takes a lot of work to keep our high bar of quality while also shipping new features and improvements. And the workload keeps increasing with the continuous growth of Rust adoption. As is unfortunately common in open source projects, a large fraction of that work is currently done by volunteers. That causes various issues, such as people burning out or complex features taking many years to ship. Unsurprisingly, one of the best ways to help improve that is to get more people who work on Rust funded! This year, several funding initiatives started ramping up, and we already experience many positive effects. They helped us improve the maintenance status of critical Rust projects and make significant progress on several long-awaited features, such as allocators, the never type, the next trait solver or the Polonius borrow checker. However, only a fraction of people working on Rust are currently funded for their work. entries.text: The rustup team is happy to announce the release of rustup version 1.29.2. Rustup is the recommended tool to install Rust, a programming language that empowers everyone to build reliable and efficient software. What's new in rustup 1.29.2 This is a small release which only updates the rustls-webpki and webpki-root-certs dependencies to address the problematic eMudhra intermediate certificates issue described in CVE-2026-111943. See also RUSTSEC-2026-0382. Further details are available in the changelog! How to update If you have a previous version of rustup installed, getting the new one is as easy as stopping any programs which may be using rustup (e.g. closing your IDE) and running: $ rustup self update Rustup will also automatically update itself at the end of a normal toolchain update: $ rustup update If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website. Rustup's documentation is also available in the rustup book. Caveats Rustup releases can come with problems not caused by rustup itself but just due to having a new release. In particular, anti-malware scanners might block rustup or stop it from creating or copying files, especially when installing rust-docs which contains many small files. Issues like this should be automatically resolved in a few weeks when the anti-malware scanners are updated to be aware of the new rustup release. Thanks Thanks again to all the contributors who made this rustup release possible!
entries.title: Announcing rustup 1.29.2

entries.text: The Rust team has published a new point release of Rust, 1.99.1. Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.99.1 is as easy as: rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website. What's in 1.99.1 Rust 1.99.1 fixes the following regressions from prior releases: Missing symbol wcslen: Some Rust targets were getting link errors for missing wcslen, and that function is now present in Rust's compiler-builtins library as a fallback. The LLVM loop-idiom-wcslen pass may introduce calls to wcslen as an optimization, and some Rust targets did not have that function readily available in libc or elsewhere. The UEFI targets in particular were broken for any project using std, as some of these calls were introduced in the precompiled standard library, but the issue was also reproducible for similar user code patterns. Miscompilation of FFI bool return values on x86_64: Rust functions returning bool through FFI could leave bits 1-7 of the return register unspecified, causing callers to observe raw values other than 0 or 1. This return type is now marked for zero-extension again, as required by the ABI. rust-lld failed to load libLLVM on macOS: This linker could fail to run if the compiler was invoked without the rustup proxy, as there was no direct setting for the appropriate library search path. entries.summary: With Rust 1.100.0, the following changes to 32-bit Windows targets will happen: i686-pc-windows-msvc Tier 1 with host tools target will be demoted to Tier 1 without host tools.
entries.text: With Rust 1.100.0, the following changes to 32-bit Windows targets will happen: i686-pc-windows-msvc Tier 1 with host tools target will be demoted to Tier 1 without host tools. i686-pc-windows-gnu Tier 2 with host tools target will be demoted to Tier 2 without host tools. Builds of the standard library will continue to be distributed, but host tools such as the compiler will be no longer available. i686-pc-windows-msvc as a Tier 1 target still undergoes CI testing. To build 32-bit Windows binaries, cross-compiling from a still-supported host toolchain (such as a 64-bit Windows ones) will be required from now on. Background Desktop and Server 32-bit only x86 CPUs are no longer sold for over 15 years, and general 32-bit Windows support has ended in October 2025. This means that the development platforms these targets are meant for hardly exist these days, and even if they do exist they typically aren't capable enough for development. Even on the modern x86_64 hardware, building i686 Windows toolchains has proven to be problematic. We have encountered compiler binaries crashing when built with the i686 MSVC target, and the GNU C++ toolchain failing with OOMs during LLVM build. Considering all these things, cross-compiling these targets from a better supported one is what we have found to be the best solution forward. Please report any bugs you might come across! What's in 1.99.0 stable extern "C" variadics Rust 1.99.0 stabilizes defining C-ABI variadic functions with "C" and "C-unwind" ABIs. Variadic functions defined this way use a variable argument list (...) and accept an arbitrary number of arguments. Rust could already call externally-defined variadic functions (e.g., libc::printf). With Rust 1.99, these functions can now be written in Rust itself: /// SAFETY: must be called with (at least) 2 i32 arguments. unsafe extern "C" fn sum(mut args: ...) -> i32 { // SAFETY: guaranteed by the caller. let a = unsafe { args.next_arg::<i32>() }; let b = unsafe { args.next_arg::<i32>() }; a + b } fn foo() -> i32 { unsafe { sum(0i32, 2i32) } } The type of ... is VaList, which is ABI-compatible with the C va_list type across targets. entries.summary: At the end of August, we announced our first Maintainers in Residence, Rust Project contributors who are funded for their upstream contributions and maintenance work from the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund (RFMF).
entries.text: At the end of August, we announced our first Maintainers in Residence, Rust Project contributors who are funded for their upstream contributions and maintenance work from the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund (RFMF). Since then, the Rust Leadership Council has dedicated more funds from its Project Priorities budget to RFMF, and together with AWS also providing additional funds, this allowed us to open a new full-time Maintainer in Residence (MiR) position to support the Cargo team. We would like to thank the Rust Leadership Council, AWS, and also the Rust Foundation for providing us with this opportunity! If you would like to help us hire more maintainers to improve Rust, consider donating to RFMF. This post explains why we chose to support the Cargo team specifically, and introduces Scott Schafer, the new Cargo Maintainer in Residence. Why Cargo? The new MiR full-time position is dedicated to helping with the maintenance of Cargo, our build system and package manager. The Cargo project is deeply involved in many new Rust features, improvements, and Project Goals. Combined with its cross-cutting nature, where it has to support many different use-cases and integrate with several other tools, it takes a lot of work just to keep up with its maintenance needs, let alone support so many feature requests and proposed changes.
